transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-10 08:30 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Leila Ortiz (Redwood SE), Oliver Hayes (ZenHouse CTO), Priya Shah (Lead ML Engineer), Marcus Lee (DevOps), Sana Gomez (Procurement)

Auto sections (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Summary: ZenHouse is evaluating a vendor swap from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together into Redwood; focused on parity for our existing endpoints, cost/latency tradeoffs, and private deployment options. They want a two-week pilot with a plan to prove SLO parity.
Topics: parity mapping, console tour, routing, KV cache, quantization, security docs
Action items: see metadata

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining. we got the agenda in the invite — parity mapping, quick console tour, and then we'll do questions and next steps. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Oliver (ZenHouse): good morning, yeah thanks. we've got Priya and Marcus on the video, and Sana from procurement will just be listening for contracting notes.
[00:12] Priya (ZenHouse): hi, hi. quick context: we run a mix of OpenAI and Anthropic endpoints for product and research. latency budgets are tight, want to avoid user regressions, and security is top of mind — some workloads need private network.
[00:23] Leila (Redwood): great, that's exactly what we wanted to hear. to make this practical we'll map their current endpoints and traffic profiles to Redwood models and runtime configs, show console settings for routing and fallbacks, and propose a pilot.
[00:34] Marcus (ZenHouse): one ask up front — we want to understand how KV cache behaves for user session workloads. right now our OpenAI setup keeps a local prefix cache and some LRU for tokens.
[00:46] Leila (Redwood): yeah, our runtime supports prefix and KV caching; it's often called KV cache but sometimes transcribed in our docs as K V cash — ha. you can pin cache keys per route, TTLs, and we have automatic prefix coalescing to avoid double work. in practice that reduces per-token compute on repeat contexts by up to 60% depending on hit rates.
[01:05] Priya: nice. what's the migration friction for prompt shapes? our prompts are long, lots of system + history.
[01:12] Ethan: good question. parity often comes down to 3 things: model choice (same family/temperature), tokenization differences, and runtime truncation/stop-seq handling. Leila will show a mapping table.
[01:21] Leila: starting console share — (screen noise) — okay, on the model catalog we ingest verified open models and vendor-provided checkpoints. for most of the OpenAI GPT-like endpoints you can map to compatible open models; for Anthropic we recommend the Anthro-equivalent open families or Redwood-verified variants. there will be edge cases with logits/penalties so we usually run A/B tests during pilot.
[01:40] Oliver: can you show an example mapping? e.g., we call openai gpt-4o for internal summarization and together model X for customer-facing chat.
[01:49] Leila: sure — here is a sample parity row: openai-gpt-4o -> redwood-4o-xx (same paramization, similar temperature defaults). together-x -> redwood-chat-x (we add a slight prompt template change to preserve persona). note: sometimes tokens shift due to tokenizer differences, so cost parity requires per-100k-token measurement.
[02:10] Priya: that token shift bit is a hard one — we saw 5-7% delta between vendors.
[02:14] Leila: yep, and quantization can change that too because smaller int8 kernels may alter per-token throughput. we recommend running the quantized profile that balances latencies for your P95 targets. you can see those perf profiles on the model detail page.
[02:30] Marcus: on dedicated vs hosted — our security team would prefer Dedicated or Private for some PHI-ish workloads. can Redwood Dedicated be inside our VPC?
[02:38] Ethan: Redwood Dedicated is customer-isolated capacity in our cloud — we provide VPC peering for Dedicated or Private deployments. Private gives you a customer-controlled control plane option for stricter compliance and on-prem. we'll share our network diagram and KMS integration notes.
[02:52] Sana (ZenHouse): procurement note — if it's Dedicated, we need lead time for contract and procurement approvals. what's typical pilot pricing?
[02:58] Ethan: for pilots we typically provide trial credits and a limited reserved pool or a trial Dedicated node depending on the scope. Leila will quantify cost parity examples after this.
[03:08] [03:10] Leila: jumping back to console — routing policies are here. you can route by latency SLO, cost tiers, or region. fallback chains let you route to a cheaper variant on overload; that's key for graceful degradation. we also show per-token cost and latency histograms at the request level in tracing.
[03:30] Oliver: curious about retries and the KV cache interplay — if a fallback hits a cheaper model, does cache invalidate or rehydrate?
[03:36] Leila: good nuance. we do not automatically evict cache on fallback; you can configure cache scope per policy. typical pattern: keep cache valid across variants when the models are compatible; otherwise set a short TTL on cross-variant routes.
[03:50] Priya: can you demo a live endpoint swap? that would make things concrete.
[03:55] Leila: yep — demo time. I'm going to invoke a sample endpoint that currently points at together-chat-x and we'll flip it to redwood-chat-x and show latency counters.
[04:06] [04:20] (demo noise)
[04:20] Leila: ok call fired — current P50 120 ms, P95 340 ms for a 1k token history. flipping to redwood-chat-x with quantization profile q8 yields P50 110 ms, P95 360 ms. cost per 1k tokens is showing slightly lower due to batching and runtime efficiencies.
[04:40] Marcus: that P95 bump worries me — 360 vs 340, how do we tune it?
[04:44] Leila: you tune batch sizes, timeout windows, and the quantization profile. also route critical paths to non-quantized instances and less critical flows to quantized ones. auto-batching has knobs for latency SLOs.
[04:56] Priya: did you say kv cache hits reduce compute by 60% earlier — that's significant. do you have sample hit-rate dashboards?
[05:03] Leila: yes, here's a breakdown — you can see hit-rate over time and the estimated token savings. common pattern: session-based chat shows high prefix hit rates so decimal savings add up.
[05:15] Oliver: security — we need KMS + HSM support for keys and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. is that supported?
[05:23] Ethan: yes — KMS integrations and HSM-supported key wraps are supported in Private and Dedicated. we stream audit logs to customer sinks and keep immutable event records. we'll attach the security whitepaper.
[05:36] Priya: latency sensitivity — our user-facing chat requires P95 under 400ms for 2k-token scenarios. can Redwood hit that at scale?
[05:44] Leila: yes, with a couple caveats: choose the right model variant, configure dedicated pool sizing, and tune batching thresholds. we also have smart routing — if one region overloads, requests can spill to another region to keep SLO.
[05:58] Marcus: how do we validate parity for quality? we run eval sets and regression tests for prompts and hallucination rates.
[06:06] Leila: recommended approach: run side-by-side A/B with identical prompts, log outputs, run automated evaluations and human spot-checks. our Optimize toolkit can surface quality regressions tied to prompt sets with alerting.
[06:18] Oliver: and how long does a typical pilot take to be convincing?
[06:22] Ethan: most pilots run 2–4 weeks. a minimal pilot includes: traffic mirroring for 1 week, A/B for 1 week, and a final checklist for security and throughput.
[06:31] Priya: traffic mirroring — do you support streaming replication from our prod cluster?
[06:35] Leila: we support request mirroring at the gateway level or SDK level. for high-throughput mirroring we recommend a sampled mirror to avoid doubling cost.
[06:44] Sana: procurement follow-up — are there any data residency constraints we should watch for?
[06:48] Ethan: yes — we host in multiple regions; Dedicated/reserved capacity can be pinned to region. Private/on-prem is available for strict residency needs.
[06:55] [07:00] (brief pause, screen share shifts)
[07:04] Leila: small demo of model detail page — you can see perf profiles: p50/p95 for different sequence lengths and CPU/GPU kernel choices, and a toggle for quantized vs full precision. also we provide recommended autoscale policies per throughput pattern.
[07:20] Priya: in our tests we saw some prompt drift when moving from together-x to their open counterparts — does Redwood provide guardrails around system/prompt templates?
[07:29] Leila: yes, we have a templating system and structured output validators to force shapes and allow exact-match checks on critical fields. that reduces drift risk.
[07:38] Marcus: integration — our stack currently uses a combination of SDK and proxy routing. will switching to Redwood require heavy SDK changes?
[07:45] Ethan: the API is REST/SDK friendly; we have adapter examples for OpenAI-compatible calls so switching routing can be as simple as changing the endpoint and small header mappings. for Together-specific features we provide shim scripts.
[07:58] Oliver: what about cost modelling — can you share an example across our monthly 100M tokens baseline?
[08:04] Leila: yes — I'll prepare a cost parity spreadsheet. rough numbers in the demo showed a small cost advantage driven by caching and batching but exact figures need accounting for tokenizer deltas and any quantization quality tradeoffs.
[08:18] Priya: edge case: some of our pipelines rely on exact logit values and temperature tuning; will logits be identical?
[08:25] Leila: logits often differ across model and tokenizer combos — we don't guarantee bit-exact logits vs vendor models. for regen-sensitive pipelines we recommend testing at pilot and possibly keeping those pipelines on vendor endpoints or using model distillation.
[08:40] Marcus: can Redwood run on our on-prem hardware for true air-gapped?
[08:44] Ethan: yep — we offer on-prem packages. that's a longer procurement cycle but supported.
[08:50] Oliver: timeline — if we wanted to kick off a pilot, what's the next step?
[08:55] Ethan: steps: 1) we share security docs and cost parity (this week), 2) ZenHouse confirms infra windows and pilot scope (Marcus), 3) we provision trial Dedicated or a small private env, 4) run two-week pilot with mirrored traffic + A/B.
[09:12] Sana: procurement will need a statement of work and pilot terms — we'll review once we have the security docs.
[09:18] Leila: quick note on instrumentation: we emit per-request traces, token-level cost, and quality metrics that you can ship to your telemetry; we also support webhook alerts on regression thresholds.
[09:29] Priya: any gotchas moving from Anthropic safety wrappers?
[09:33] Leila: our runtime supports safety layers and you can layer custom filters. there may be differences in vendor-provided red-teaming results; we recommend parallel evals.
[09:41] Oliver: ok let's capture next steps — we'll want the parity spreadsheet and security package, Marcus will confirm infra access, and we'll aim for a kickoff the week of March 21 if procurement clears.
[09:52] Ethan: perfect. I'll send meeting notes and the security pack. Leila will share the cost parity sheet and a suggested pilot config.
[09:59] Marcus: one small Q — how do rollbacks look if we see quality degradation in prod?
[10:03] Leila: the console supports instant rollbacks and can route a percentage of traffic back to the prior vendor via the fallback chain; you can also do canaries and A/B weights.
[10:12] Priya: please include a sample rollback playbook in the doc set.
[10:15] Ethan: will do.
[10:18] (wrap-up)
[10:19] Oliver: thanks, this was super helpful. we have what we need to start internal scoring. thanks to Leila and Ethan.
[10:23] Sana: thanks everyone.
[10:25] Ethan: thanks all — we'll follow up by EOD with docs and the proposed schedule.

(End of transcript)
